heroIntro: Every business owner's worst nightmare is discovering that a trusted accountant, store manager, procurement executive, or cashier has systematically siphoned corporate funds for months or years. In Bangladesh, internal financial fraud takes many forms: manipulating ERP accounting software, fabricating fake vendor invoices, skimming customer cash payments, diverting collection cheques into personal accounts, or creating ghost employees. When confronted, dishonest employees often resign abruptly, destroy ledgers, or threaten counter-cases of wrongful termination. The Penal Code 1860 and the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 provide severe, specialized criminal sanctions for white-collar workplace theft. Under Section 408, employee embezzlement is a non-bailable offense carrying up to 7 years rigorous imprisonment. Here is the definitive legal playbook for business owners to preserve forensic evidence, file an unshakeable FIR, and recover stolen corporate capital.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: What Legal Action Can an Employer Take for Employee Embezzlement in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: When an employee steals company funds or property, the employer can initiate immediate criminal and civil proceedings. Under Section 408 of the Penal Code 1860 (Criminal Breach of Trust by Clerk or Servant), employee embezzlement is a cognizable and non-bailable offense punishable by up to seven (7) years rigorous imprisonment plus heavy fines. If the employee cooked books or manipulated accounting software, they face additional charges under Section 477A (Falsification of Accounts, up to 7 years) and Section 420 (Cheating). The employer must conduct an immediate internal audit, secure digital logs, and file an FIR at the local Thana or a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Metropolitan Magistrate Court, while concurrently filing an application for pre-judgment attachment of the employee's personal bank accounts and assets under Order 38 CPC.
highlights: Section 408 Penal Code 1860 specifically targets dishonest misappropriation by employees with up to 7 years imprisonment.
Section 477A penalizes falsification of accounts, alteration of books, and manipulation of digital billing systems.
Employee embezzlement is non-bailable, allowing police to immediately arrest the accused upon registration of an FIR.
Civil courts can attach the dishonest employee's personal property and bank accounts to enforce full restitution.
points: Step 1: Immediately revoke all system access cards, software passwords, and bank authorizations without tipping off the employee.
Step 2: Engage an independent chartered accountant to conduct a rapid forensic audit and establish the exact missing sum.
Step 3: Secure original financial evidence: manipulated vouchers, fake bank deposit slips, and ERP database audit trails.
Step 4: File a formal FIR at the local Thana or a CR case under Sections 408, 420, and 477A of the Penal Code 1860.

sections.title: The Growing Epidemic of Workplace Embezzlement in Bangladesh
sections.content:
As businesses expand across Bangladesh's manufacturing, retail, e-commerce, and logistics sectors, corporate owners are forced to delegate financial authority. Managers handle petty cash, accountants manage online banking tokens, and sales executives collect cash on delivery (COD) from retail distribution networks. Unfortunately, weak internal controls and misplaced personal trust create fertile ground for systematic embezzlement.

Employers often discover the fraud accidentally: an unexpected tax audit reveals discrepancies, a supplier issues a legal notice for unpaid invoices that were purportedly cleared months ago, or an accountant fails to report to work, leaving behind a trail of fabricated bank challans. When the scale of theft is uncovered—frequently totaling tens of lakhs or crores of taka—business owners panic. Taking emotional steps, such as physically confining the employee or seizing their family's belongings, exposes the employer to retaliatory extortion and kidnapping allegations. Recovering stolen funds requires disciplined, strategic execution of statutory criminal and civil procedures.

sections.title: Penal Code Section 408: Criminal Breach of Trust by Clerk or Servant
sections.content:
The core statutory weapon against internal employee theft is Section 408 of the Penal Code 1860. While Section 406 covers general criminal breach of trust (carrying up to 3 years imprisonment), Section 408 recognizes that employees occupy a special position of trust and fiduciary duty, prescribing far harsher penalties:

'Whoever, being a clerk or servant or employed as a clerk or servant, and being in any manner entrusted in such capacity with property, or with any dominion over property, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of that property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.'

To secure a conviction under Section 408, the prosecution must establish three essential legal ingredients: (1) that the accused was an employee (clerk, manager, officer, or servant) of the complainant; (2) that the accused was entrusted with the company's property, cash, or financial dominion; and (3) that the accused dishonestly misappropriated, converted to their own use, or disposed of that property in violation of company rules. Offenses under Section 408 are cognizable, meaning police have statutory authority to arrest the employee without an arrest warrant.

sections.title: Section 477A: Falsification of Accounts and Ledgers
sections.content:
Embezzlement rarely occurs without documentary concealment. To mask stolen funds, dishonest employees routinely falsify accounting ledgers, forge bank deposit slips, alter invoices, or delete digital sales records. To penalize this administrative deception, prosecutors invoke Section 477A of the Penal Code 1860 (Falsification of Accounts).

Section 477A provides that whoever, being a clerk, officer, or servant, willfully and with intent to defraud, destroys, alters, mutilates, or falsifies any book, paper, writing, valuable security, or account belonging to their employer, or makes false entries therein, shall be punished with imprisonment for up to seven (7) years, or with fine, or with both. Combining Section 408 (theft of money) with Section 477A (cooking the books) and Section 420 (cheating) creates a formidable, multi-layered criminal charge sheet that withstands defense scrutiny in the Magistrate Court.

sections.title: First 24 Hours: Internal Investigation and Evidence Lockdown
sections.content:
The actions an employer takes within the first 24 hours of uncovering embezzlement determine whether the stolen money will be recovered or lost forever. A disciplined protocol must be executed immediately:

  1. Digital Access Lockdown: Instantly revoke the suspect employee's access to enterprise software (Tally, SAP, Oracle), corporate email accounts, and cloud storage. Freeze any banking tokens, digital signature devices, or mobile financial service (MFS) agent SIMs held by the employee.
  2. Forensic Physical Seizure: Under the supervision of two neutral company witnesses, secure the employee's work desk, desktop computer, hard drives, physical voucher files, and chequebooks. Create a formal seizure inventory list signed by both witnesses.
  3. Emergency Forensic Audit: Retain an independent chartered accountant or certified fraud examiner to review the suspected transaction window, verify bank statements directly from the bank branch, and issue an expedited Audit Discrepancy Report.

Never alert or confront the employee until this documentary evidence is securely backed up off-site.

sections.title: Drafting the FIR at the Thana vs. Filing a CR Case
sections.content:
Once the audit report confirms the missing sums, the employer must initiate formal criminal prosecution. The employer has two statutory pathways:

  • First Information Report (FIR) at the Local Thana: The company's authorized representative (backed by a Board Resolution) submits a written complaint to the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the Thana having territorial jurisdiction over the office. Because Section 408 is a cognizable offense, the police are legally required to register it as an FIR under Section 154 CrPC, initiate an immediate investigation, and apprehend the suspect.
  • Complaint Register (CR) Case Before the Magistrate Court: If the local Thana delays or hesitates to register the FIR due to jurisdictional squabbles, the advocate files a direct petition before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) Court under Section 190 CrPC. The Magistrate examines the complainant under Section 200 CrPC, reviews the audit exhibits, and directs the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) or Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) to conduct a specialized inquiry.

sections.title: Police Investigation, Arrest, and Bail Opposition
sections.content:
Following the registration of the case, the investigating officer (IO) executes search and seizure protocols. Under Section 165 CrPC, the IO can search the accused employee's residence, seize passbooks, cash, luxury vehicles purchased with embezzled proceeds, and laptop computers. The IO also issues official requisitions under Section 94 CrPC to commercial banks to freeze the employee's personal and familial bank accounts.

When the accused is arrested and produced before the Magistrate, their defense counsel routinely moves for bail. The employer's advocate must fiercely oppose bail: arguing that Section 408 is a non-bailable offense, that the stolen corporate funds have not yet been recovered, and that the accused possesses access to digital evidence that could be tampered with if released. Sustained detention in custody frequently compels the accused's family to offer restitution of the embezzled sums in exchange for a compromise.

sections.title: Asset Tracing and Civil Recovery: Money Suits and Injunctions
sections.content:
While criminal prosecution penalizes the dishonest employee with prison time, a criminal court does not automatically write a cheque refunding the company's stolen millions. To achieve complete financial recovery, corporate legal counsel institutes parallel civil proceedings:

  1. Money Suit for Restitution: The company files a formal Money Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge claiming the exact embezzled sum plus interest, damages, and forensic audit expenses.
  2. Attachment Before Judgment (Order 38 Rule 5 CPC): The advocate immediately petitions the civil court to attach the employee's personal real estate, family residential flats, vehicles, and fixed deposits purchased with stolen proceeds.
  3. Bank Account Injunctions: The civil court issues injunctions restraining commercial banks from permitting the employee or their nominee spouses from withdrawing or transferring funds.

Operating civil asset attachment alongside criminal custody creates unbearable pressure, ensuring that stolen corporate capital is recovered.

sections.content:
The table below highlights the crucial distinctions between workplace embezzlement under Section 408 and general theft or cheating under the Penal Code:

Utilizing Section 408 ensures that the judicial system treats workplace theft with the severity it warrants.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Cracking an Accountant's Fraud Ring in Gazipur
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how aggressive corporate prosecution dismantled an embezzlement ring in Gazipur:

A textile spinning mill in Gazipur employed a senior accountant for over five years, entrusting him with preparing monthly utility payments, vendor cheques, and local raw cotton procurement disbursements. Over an eighteen-month period, the accountant conspired with an external supplier to generate inflated cotton procurement invoices, diverting BDT 42,00,000 into a newly opened bank account registered under his wife's maiden name, while altering the company's internal ERP ledger entries to display 'full vendor settlement.'

During an unannounced internal audit, the mill's managing director discovered that vendor balances were still outstanding. Rather than confronting the accountant, the company retained a corporate criminal advocate. Within 48 hours, the advocate oversaw a forensic IT backup of the ERP server, secured original altered cheques from the company's bank branch, and compiled an unshakeable audit dossier. The advocate then drafted an FIR submitted directly to the Gazipur Police, registered under Sections 408, 420, and 477A of the Penal Code.

Police arrested the accountant at his residence, seizing bank passbooks showing BDT 25,00,000 in fixed deposits and documents for a newly purchased residential plot in Gazipur. Concurrently, the advocate filed an emergency petition before the Joint District Judge Court under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC, securing an attachment order against the accountant's newly acquired land and bank accounts. Confronted with sustained criminal detention and total asset freezing, the accountant's family negotiated a complete restitution agreement: the BDT 25,00,000 bank balance was transferred back to the mill, and the residential plot was surrendered to settle the remaining debt, achieving 100% financial recovery for the enterprise.

faqs.question: What is the punishment for employee embezzlement in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under Section 408 of the Penal Code 1860, criminal breach of trust by a clerk or servant is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for up to seven (7) years and a monetary fine. If accompanied by falsification of accounts under Section 477A, an additional sentence of up to 7 years may be imposed.

faqs.question: Is employee embezzlement a bailable offense in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Section 408 of the Penal Code is a non-bailable offense. The police can arrest the employee without a warrant, and obtaining bail from the Magistrate Court is difficult, particularly when substantial sums remain unrecovered.

faqs.question: Can an employer deduct stolen money from an employee's salary or provident fund?
faqs.answer: Under the Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, unilateral salary deductions are restricted unless formal disciplinary proceedings and an inquiry committee find the employee guilty of misconduct. To safely recover stolen funds without labor tribunal complications, filing a civil Money Suit with Order 38 attachment is the recommended legal route.

faqs.question: What evidence is needed to prove employee embezzlement?
faqs.answer: You need the appointment letter proving employment, proof of entrustment (job description or authorization), original altered receipts or forged vouchers, certified bank statements showing unauthorized transfers, and an independent chartered accountant's audit report.

faqs.question: Can police freeze an employee's personal bank account during investigation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the investigating officer has the legal authority to issue formal written orders to commercial banks to freeze the suspect's accounts and provide detailed transaction histories.

faqs.question: What should I do if an embezzling employee resigns and disappears?
faqs.answer: Immediately lodge an FIR at the local Thana. The police will track the accused through lawful mobile tower location and NID databases. If the accused absconds, the court will issue arrest warrants and proclamation/attachment orders under Sections 87 and 88 CrPC.

faqs.question: Can an employer file a case against an employee's family member who received stolen money?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the employee transferred embezzled corporate funds into their spouse's or relative's personal bank accounts, those individuals can be charged under Section 411 of the Penal Code (dishonestly receiving stolen property) or as conspirators under Section 109.

faqs.question: Can an overseas company operating in Bangladesh prosecute a local employee for fraud?
faqs.answer: Yes. A multinational corporation or overseas investor can authorize a local managing director, country manager, or lawyer via a formal Board Resolution or Power of Attorney to institute criminal and civil proceedings against dishonest local personnel.
